1.pericope_label: Blow ye the trumpet in Zion, and sound an alarm in my holy mountain: let all the inhabitants of the land tremble: for the day of the Lord cometh, for it is nigh at hand; A day of darkness and of gloominess, a day of clouds and of thick darkness, as the morning spread upon the mountains: a great people and a strong; there hath not been ever the like, neither shall be any more after it, even to the years of many generations.

schools.summary: Take the alarm as pointing past the locusts to a mustering of hostile nations, and argue from the root that the morning clause means blackness rather than dawn.
Explain why punishment is set before the eyes and treat the eleven verses as one movement designed to stir the people by fear.
Give the plan of the chapter and supply travellers' reports of the insects themselves.
Stresses the security the alarm interrupts and locates the judgment among the plagues written in the law.

debates.question: Does the morning spread on the mountains mean dawn or blackness?

positions.position: Dawn, and the point is speed, since it spreads in a moment over the mountains.
Dawn, spreading over the whole hemisphere and first on the high mountains, as the calamities overspread the people.
Blackness: the root means both to become black and to break forth as light, and the context suits a thick dark cloud settled on the mountain top.
The received rendering stands, morning dawn spread over the mountains.

outliers.claim: Denies that this is a fresh address, making it the second part of one sermon of repentance that repeats a command already hinted at in the previous chapter.

themes: Blow ye the trumpet in Zion, and sound an alarm in my holy mountain: let all the inhabitants of the land tremble: for the day of the Lord cometh, for it is nigh at hand;

A day of darkness and of gloominess, a day of clouds and of thick darkness, as the morning spread upon the mountains: a great people and a strong; there hath not been ever the like, neither shall be any more after it, even to the years of many generations.

3.pericope_label: A fire devoureth before them; and behind them a flame burneth: the land is as the garden of Eden before them, and behind them a desolate wilderness; yea, and nothing shall escape them. The appearance of them is as the appearance of horses; and as horsemen, so shall they run. Like the noise of chariots on the tops of mountains shall they leap, like the noise of a flame of fire that devoureth the stubble, as a strong people set in battle array. Before their face the people shall be much pained: all faces shall gather blackness. They shall run like mighty men; they shall climb the wall like men of war; and they shall march every one on his ways, and they shall not break their ranks:

schools.summary: Apply the figure to the invading hosts and find the same comparison to horses in the apocalypse.
Decline the natural history for the doctrine, taking the passage for finality of judgment and suddenness of vengeance.
Supply travellers' and naturalists' testimony throughout, and caution that the prophet says the locusts resemble men of war rather than are them.

debates.question: How literally should the military comparisons be taken?

positions.position: The prophet does not say they are men of war but that they resemble them, being locusts and only in their operations like the rest.
The skill in ordering and steadiness in rank foretell the terror of both the armies signified and the locusts themselves.
The similitudes need little explanation; the point is the suddenness of the vengeance, distance being no obstacle.
The comparison to a well-ordered host runs through the whole passage.

outliers.claim: Sets out three renderings of the blackness of faces and records a marginal alternative, adopted by the Greek and Latin versions and by a reformer, which reads pot instead, resting on the similarity of the Hebrew words.
Explains the leaping from anatomy, the hindmost legs being longest, citing a naturalist for the rule that insects with long hind legs leap.

themes: A fire devoureth before them; and behind them a flame burneth: the land is as the garden of Eden before them, and behind them a desolate wilderness; yea, and nothing shall escape them.
The appearance of them is as the appearance of horses; and as horsemen, so shall they run.
Like the noise of chariots on the tops of mountains shall they leap, like the noise of a flame of fire that devoureth the stubble, as a strong people set in battle array.
Before their face the people shall be much pained: all faces shall gather blackness.
They shall run like mighty men; they shall climb the wall like men of war; and they shall march every one on his ways, and they shall not break their ranks:

8.pericope_label: Neither shall one thrust another; they shall walk every one in his path: and when they fall upon the sword, they shall not be wounded. They shall run to and fro in the city; they shall run upon the wall, they shall climb up upon the houses; they shall enter in at the windows like a thief. The earth shall quake before them; the heavens shall tremble: the sun and the moon shall be dark, and the stars shall withdraw their shining: And the Lord shall utter his voice before his army: for his camp is very great: for he is strong that executeth his word: for the day of the Lord is great and very terrible; and who can abide it?

schools.summary: Rejects the label of hyperbole for the shaking of earth and heaven, making it the presence and judgment of God that causes the trepidation.
Grants the hyperbole and defends it, since the prophet addressed men extremely stupid who could not be touched by ordinary speech.
Distinguish soldiers from insects in the running to and fro, and turn the poetical expressions prettily.

debates.question: Is the shaking of earth and heaven hyperbole?

positions.position: No: it is the presence and judgment of God, his voice in the thunder, that causes the trepidation.
Yes, and rightly so, since it avails nothing to speak ordinarily to perverse men whom Satan has fascinated.
Poetical expressions of universal consternation, with a physical basis in a swarm that obscures the heavens for twelve miles.
A divine hyperbole which may yet refer to the great day.

outliers.claim: Makes the unbroken march concrete: an army can hardly march without tumult as two or three men walk together, and when a hundred horsemen move together some commonly hinder others.
Reports that a Roman naturalist called the locusts the plague of the gods and that the Arabians style them the army of God, with a tradition about an inscription on their wings.

themes: Neither shall one thrust another; they shall walk every one in his path: and when they fall upon the sword, they shall not be wounded.
They shall run to and fro in the city; they shall run upon the wall, they shall climb up upon the houses; they shall enter in at the windows like a thief.
The earth shall quake before them; the heavens shall tremble: the sun and the moon shall be dark, and the stars shall withdraw their shining:
And the Lord shall utter his voice before his army: for his camp is very great: for he is strong that executeth his word: for the day of the Lord is great and very terrible; and who can abide it?

12.pericope_label: Therefore also now, saith the Lord, turn ye even to me with all your heart, and with fasting, and with weeping, and with mourning: And rend your heart, and not your garments, and turn unto the Lord your God: for he is gracious and merciful, slow to anger, and of great kindness, and repenteth him of the evil.

schools.summary: Notes that the word rendered saith is no common word but implies an authoritative utterance, and states that the judgments of God, like his mercies, are conditional.
Grounds the exhortation in the hope of pardon, since one who despairs disregards himself entirely, and makes ceremony without a sincere heart mere mockery.
Counts three means of turning and warns that external worship will only increase the evil.
Reads the exhortation as answering the end for which the judgment was sent and as able to stay its progress.

debates.question: Is the rending of garments forbidden?

positions.position: Not absolutely but comparatively: it was neither criminal nor unlawful, the apostles having used it, but the heart must be rent rather than the garments only.
External worship and hypocritical pretension will only increase the evil and bring heavier judgments.
All ceremonies are mere mockeries when a sincere heart does not precede them; God has become insensible to these customs.

outliers.claim: States the principle behind the divine repenting: it means that of his own will he would not the death of a sinner, the judgments of God being conditional like his mercies.
Notes that the prophet concludes by repeating the appeal for a solemn meeting in order to make the admonition still more emphatic.

themes: Therefore also now, saith the Lord, turn ye even to me with all your heart, and with fasting, and with weeping, and with mourning:
And rend your heart, and not your garments, and turn unto the Lord your God: for he is gracious and merciful, slow to anger, and of great kindness, and repenteth him of the evil.

14.pericope_label: Who knoweth if he will return and repent, and leave a blessing behind him; even a meat offering and a drink offering unto the Lord your God? Blow the trumpet in Zion, sanctify a fast, call a solemn assembly: Gather the people, sanctify the congregation, assemble the elders, gather the children, and those that suck the breasts: let the bridegroom go forth of his chamber, and the bride out of her closet.

schools.summary: Makes the returning favour the restoration of the daily sacrifices which had failed through the visitation.
Faces the difficulty that the question who knows seems to withdraw the hope just offered, and works the philology of the word for the assembly.
Explain the language of God returning and withdrawing, and give each summoned class its own reason for attending.
States the transaction as a rule of prayer, God waiting to be gracious and answering with comfortable words.

positions.position: Possibly man: whoever knows the ways of repentance will return, or he who knows iniquity lies on him, per three Jewish commentators and the Targum.
God, who does not move from place to place but is said to withdraw when he withholds blessings and to return when he gives them.
God, who may yet interpose so far that there is food for men and cattle and offerings for the temple.
God: exhortations to repentance would be useless unless he testified that he is ready to be reconciled.

outliers.claim: Works the philology of the word for assembly, which is not properly an assembly but a restraint, from labour as well as food, and so comes to designate a feast-day.

themes: Who knoweth if he will return and repent, and leave a blessing behind him; even a meat offering and a drink offering unto the Lord your God?
Blow the trumpet in Zion, sanctify a fast, call a solemn assembly:
Gather the people, sanctify the congregation, assemble the elders, gather the children, and those that suck the breasts: let the bridegroom go forth of his chamber, and the bride out of her closet.

17.pericope_label: Let the priests, the ministers of the Lord, weep between the porch and the altar, and let them say, Spare thy people, O Lord, and give not thine heritage to reproach, that the heathen should rule over them: wherefore should they say among the people, Where is their God? Then will the Lord be jealous for his land, and pity his people. Yea, the Lord will answer and say unto his people, Behold, I will send you corn, and wine, and oil, and ye shall be satisfied therewith: and I will no more make you a reproach among the heathen:

schools.summary: Observes that all mention of the locusts is now dropped, the lesser calamity swallowed up in the greater.
Uses the priests' station for a doctrine of mediation and objects that the answering verb must be future, not past.
Fix the topography of porch and altar and remove the doubt from the promise, which is no peradventure.
Makes the exchange a rule of prayer, God meeting the humbled immediately with favours.

debates.question: Should the verb of answering be past or future?

positions.position: Future: it stands in the same case as the verb for being jealous, and the comment founded on the past rendering is too refined for this place.
The past may be kept, God answering while they were still praying or as soon as they cried.

outliers.claim: Grounds the mercy in the covenant rather than the people: the title of heritage proceeds from nothing but God's gratuitous covenant, the Jews being not more excellent than others.
Places the priests between porch and altar with an open space of fifteen or twenty cubits, where the atonement sacrifice was brought and the high priest laid his hands on the victim.

themes: Let the priests, the ministers of the Lord, weep between the porch and the altar, and let them say, Spare thy people, O Lord, and give not thine heritage to reproach, that the heathen should rule over them: wherefore should they say among the people, Where is their God?
Then will the Lord be jealous for his land, and pity his people.
Yea, the Lord will answer and say unto his people, Behold, I will send you corn, and wine, and oil, and ye shall be satisfied therewith: and I will no more make you a reproach among the heathen:

20.pericope_label: But I will remove far off from you the northern army, and will drive him into a land barren and desolate, with his face toward the east sea, and his hinder part toward the utmost sea, and his stink shall come up, and his ill savour shall come up, because he hath done great things. Fear not, O land; be glad and rejoice: for the Lord will do great things. Be not afraid, ye beasts of the field: for the pastures of the wilderness do spring, for the tree beareth her fruit, the fig tree and the vine do yield their strength.

schools.summary: Calls the northern direction an exception to the usual flight of locusts, and reads the summons to land and beasts as a formal reversal of the curse.
Reads the verse as quieting a fear the promise alone could not meet, and explains why beasts are addressed at all.
Divide the army topographically between the two seas and identify the two possible reasons for calling it northern.

debates.question: Why is the invader called the northern one?

positions.position: The locusts came from the northern corner, per two Jewish commentators; the rabbis interpret it instead of the evil imagination in the heart.
Either the locusts entered by the north, or they are so called because they spread terror like the Assyrian armies that entered by the north.
An exception to the usual direction of locust flight, but literally applicable to the Assyrian hordes, whom the Jews spoke of as dwelling in the north.
That part of the locusts toward the north, the van driven into the eastern sea and the rear into the western.

outliers.claim: Turns the closing clause into a contrast: God seems for a time to lie still, waiting to see the tendency of the Satanic madness of those who rise against him, and then at length comes forth.

themes: But I will remove far off from you the northern army, and will drive him into a land barren and desolate, with his face toward the east sea, and his hinder part toward the utmost sea, and his stink shall come up, and his ill savour shall come up, because he hath done great things.
Fear not, O land; be glad and rejoice: for the Lord will do great things.
Be not afraid, ye beasts of the field: for the pastures of the wilderness do spring, for the tree beareth her fruit, the fig tree and the vine do yield their strength.

23.pericope_label: Be glad then, ye children of Zion, and rejoice in the Lord your God: for he hath given you the former rain moderately, and he will cause to come down for you the rain, the former rain, and the latter rain in the first month.

schools.summary: Notices that the rejoicing is to be manifested where the trumpet had sounded for the fast, and canvasses whether the received sense of moderately can be got out of the Hebrew.
Distinguishes the joy of the children of Zion from that of the beasts, whose joy terminates in its object.
Render the phrase as the former rain in righteousness and distinguish the two rains by their office.

debates.question: What does the former rain given moderately mean?

positions.position: In righteousness, that is, in due time and in just proportion, the rain falling after autumn and the other in spring.
The autumn rain mellows the earth for the corn and the latter ripens the fruits, the husbandmen reckoning from seed time to harvest.
Doubtful whether the received sense can be got out of the Hebrew at all.

outliers.claim: Distinguishes the joy commanded here from that of the land and the beasts: brute animals cannot raise their thoughts higher than their food, whereas God himself is set before the Jews as the ground of theirs.

themes: Be glad then, ye children of Zion, and rejoice in the Lord your God: for he hath given you the former rain moderately, and he will cause to come down for you the rain, the former rain, and the latter rain in the first month.

24.pericope_label: And the floors shall be full of wheat, and the fats shall overflow with wine and oil. And I will restore to you the years that the locust hath eaten, the cankerworm, and the caterpiller, and the palmerworm, my great army which I sent among you. And ye shall eat in plenty, and be satisfied, and praise the name of the Lord your God, that hath dealt wondrously with you: and my people shall never be ashamed. And ye shall know that I am in the midst of Israel, and that I am the Lord your God, and none else: and my people shall never be ashamed.

schools.summary: Defines the restored years as those the land would in the ordinary course of nature have needed to recover, and notes the rhetorical rounding-off of the section.
Argues from opposites that God can as easily restore fruitfulness as he made the land barren, and makes the praise the proof of true repentance.
Recalls that the insects barked the trees so that they did not recover for years, and measures the wonder arithmetically.

debates.question: Are the full floors literal or spiritual?

positions.position: Literal: when the earth is satiated with moisture it brings forth rich fruit.
The churches of Christ, set up by the preaching of the gospel and filled with souls compared to wheat.
A miraculous restoration of the land after a great devastation.

outliers.claim: Measures the wonder arithmetically, one year giving as much as the locusts had wasted in the years before, and glosses the promise against shame as freedom from seeking relief among the heathen.
Observes that the assurance of God in the midst of Israel is similar to the one closing the whole book and prepares the way for the spiritual blessings about to be announced.

themes: And the floors shall be full of wheat, and the fats shall overflow with wine and oil.
And I will restore to you the years that the locust hath eaten, the cankerworm, and the caterpiller, and the palmerworm, my great army which I sent among you.
And ye shall eat in plenty, and be satisfied, and praise the name of the Lord your God, that hath dealt wondrously with you: and my people shall never be ashamed.
And ye shall know that I am in the midst of Israel, and that I am the Lord your God, and none else: and my people shall never be ashamed.

28.pericope_label: And it shall come to pass afterward, that I will pour out my spirit upon all flesh; and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy, your old men shall dream dreams, your young men shall see visions:

schools.summary: Makes scripture its own interpreter here, tracking the changes the apostle makes in quoting the verse.
Explains why earthly blessings were promised first, since men rise to things above with great difficulty.
Argue the fulfilment historically and distinguish extraordinary gifts on the first preachers from graces given to all believers.
Warns that we must not rest in corn and wine and oil, God having reserved better things.

positions.position: After the gospel rain in the ministry of the Baptist and the apostles; three Jewish commentators refer it to time to come and to the days of the Messiah.
After this, that is, the latter days; and no such effusion took place from the prophet's day until Pentecost.
In the last days, as the apostle renders it, that is, in the Christian dispensation.
After the return out of Babylon and the troubles and salvations by which they might know the Lord.

outliers.claim: Defends the order of the chapter against the rule that the kingdom of God is to be sought first: the prophet mentioned outward benefits first because men's perceptions are slow and they are slothful in seeking spiritual life.

themes: And it shall come to pass afterward, that I will pour out my spirit upon all flesh; and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy, your old men shall dream dreams, your young men shall see visions:

29.pericope_label: And also upon the servants and upon the handmaids in those days will I pour out my spirit. And I will shew wonders in the heavens and in the earth, blood, and fire, and pillars of smoke.

schools.summary: Cites the apostle's inference that they shall prophesy, and distinguishes who feels the day of the Lord as terrible.
Finds a grammatical difficulty in the amplifying particle, which seems to narrow to a few what was just made common to all.
Make the extension a rule against restricting teaching to any class, and report the prodigies from the historians.

debates.question: What are the wonders in heaven and earth?

positions.position: Prodigies before the destruction of Jerusalem: comets, a star like a sword over the city, armies seen in battle, a flame in the temple and a voice saying let us go hence.
The portents attending the overthrow of the Jewish polity and the establishment of the Christian religion in the empire.
Fulfilled to the letter, the blood possibly an eruption such as some fountains have shown, the fire either from the earth or lightning in the air.
A sequence that seems to contradict the promise, since the prophet had been elevating the spirits of a people in the greatest sorrow.

outliers.claim: Notes that the amplifying particle makes the verse seem to limit to servants and handmaids a gift just promised to all flesh, whereas without it the clause would simply have explained the former statement.
Sets the promise expressly against a rabbinic maxim that the divine presence rests only on a man who is wise and mighty and rich.

themes: And also upon the servants and upon the handmaids in those days will I pour out my spirit.
And I will shew wonders in the heavens and in the earth, blood, and fire, and pillars of smoke.

31.pericope_label: The sun shall be turned into darkness, and the moon into blood, before the great and the terrible day of the Lord come.

schools.summary: Takes blood and darkness metaphorically for a disordered state of things and shows how the tokens of wrath harmonize with the manifestation of Christ.
Read the signs of the Jewish polity's destruction, one dating the terrible day to the sacking of the city and calling it perhaps the greatest ever shown.

debates.question: Are the darkened sun and bloodied moon literal?

positions.position: Not eclipses but smoke from burning cities, though a figurative sense of the nation's civil and ecclesiastical change is also allowed.
Figurative: the Jewish polity, civil and ecclesiastical, entirely destroyed.
Metaphorical for a disordered state of things, calamities being often compared to darkness.
Signs in heaven answering the prodigies on earth, the terrible day typifying the day of judgment.

outliers.claim: Judges the destruction of the city perhaps the greatest and most terrible day of God's vengeance ever shown to the world, or that ever will be, until the general judgment.

themes: The sun shall be turned into darkness, and the moon into blood, before the great and the terrible day of the Lord come.

32.pericope_label: And it shall come to pass, that whosoever shall call on the name of the Lord shall be delivered: for in mount Zion and in Jerusalem shall be deliverance, as the Lord hath said, and in the remnant whom the Lord shall call.

schools.summary: Corrects the noun to those that escape and follows the apostle in transferring the reference to the Messianic advent and the abolition of the difference between Jew and Greek.
Explains the placement, the calamities having been denounced to stimulate men to seek God before the assurance of salvation is added.
Argue from the apostle's use that the name invoked is Christ's, and read the place-names of the true and mystical church.

debates.question: How far does the deliverance reach?

positions.position: To the believers who withdrew from the city before its fall, and also to spiritual deliverance from sin and the wrath to come.
Beyond the safety of Christians in the war, as one scholar would limit it, to every man who invokes God for mercy in the name of Jesus.
To all who call, without the difference between Jew and Greek, their names inscribed as citizens of Zion.
Either from outward afflictions or, infinitely better, from the eternal miseries that will swallow up the unbelieving world.

outliers.claim: Adds that it will aggravate the ruin of those who perish that they might have been saved on such easy terms, then asks whether it is easy for one not elect to repent and believe, or whether he might as easily pull the sun out of the firmament.

themes: And it shall come to pass, that whosoever shall call on the name of the Lord shall be delivered: for in mount Zion and in Jerusalem shall be deliverance, as the Lord hath said, and in the remnant whom the Lord shall call.
